sections.title: Banking on Seeds
sections.intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

texts.heading: Banking on Seeds
texts.subheading: How scientists are safeguarding the world’s crop diversity

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For thousands of years, farmers sowed seed saved from their own harvests, selecting it from the plants that had performed best. Over generations, this simple practice produced an extraordinary range of local crop types, known as landraces, each suited to a particular soil, climate and set of pests. During the twentieth century, however, much of this variety disappeared as farmers switched to a far smaller number of modern, high-yielding varieties. These produced much bigger harvests, but they carried a hidden danger: when every plant in a field has almost the same genetic make-up, a single disease can sweep through the entire crop. The Irish potato famine of the 1840s is the best-known example; the lesson was repeated in 1970, when a fungal disease spread through maize fields in the United States, where most of the hybrids grown shared one inherited trait that left them exposed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Plant scientists responded by collecting as many varieties as possible before they vanished and storing them in gene banks. There are now well over a thousand such banks worldwide, some holding several hundred thousand samples. Alongside landraces, many also keep the wild relatives of crops — species that have never been domesticated but may carry genes for tolerating drought, heat or salty soil. For plant breeders, these collections work like a library of useful traits: when a new disease appears, or a crop must cope with a hotter climate, they can search them for plants that already possess the qualities they need.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The routine at the Ardley Seed Centre is typical. Each incoming sample is cleaned, checked for pests and disease, and counted. The seeds are then dried slowly in a room where the humidity is kept very low, until only about five per cent of their weight is water. Staff regard this as the most important step, because any water remaining inside would turn into ice crystals when the seeds were frozen, rupturing their cells. Once dry, the seeds are sealed in airtight foil packets and placed in a cold store at around minus 18 degrees Celsius. Under these conditions, the seeds of many crops remain alive for decades, and those of some species should survive far longer.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not every plant fits this system. The seeds of most cereals and pulses tolerate drying and are described as ‘orthodox’. However, the seeds of many tropical species, including cocoa and mango, are killed by drying; botanists call such seeds ‘recalcitrant’, and they cannot be banked in the usual way. A different problem arises with crops such as potatoes, cassava and bananas, which are normally grown from pieces of a parent plant rather than from seed. These are usually conserved as living plants in field collections, as tiny plantlets in test tubes, or by cryopreservation, in which small pieces of tissue are frozen in liquid nitrogen at about minus 196 degrees.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even in cold storage, seeds gradually lose their ability to germinate. At Ardley, staff therefore test every sample once a decade by sowing a few of its seeds and counting how many sprout. When the proportion falls below a fixed threshold, the sample must be regenerated: planted out, grown to maturity and harvested to provide fresh seed. The centre’s managers describe regeneration as the most costly and risky part of their work. Cross-pollinating plants such as maize must be kept apart so that they do not breed with neighbouring varieties, and if too few plants are grown, some of the original genetic variation may be lost. Labelling errors can also creep in when hundreds of samples are handled in one season.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Gene banks are themselves vulnerable. Collections have been damaged by floods and typhoons, destroyed or looted during wars, and lost more gradually through power failures and lack of funding. Banks are therefore encouraged to send duplicate samples to a second, distant site. The best-known back-up store is a vault cut deep into a mountainside on a remote Arctic island; it opened in 2008. Duplicates are kept there in sealed boxes that remain the property of the depositing institutions; the vault’s own staff never open them. Since the surrounding ground is permanently frozen, the samples would stay below freezing point even if the cooling equipment failed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Such duplication has already proved its worth. In 2015, an agricultural research centre that civil war had forced to leave its headquarters in Syria became the first institution to withdraw seeds from the Arctic vault, using them to rebuild its working collections in two other countries; it later sent freshly grown seed back to the vault. An older episode shows the devotion such collections can inspire. During the siege of Leningrad in the Second World War, several of the scientists guarding the city’s famous seed collection are said to have starved to death rather than eat the seeds and tubers in their care.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Not everyone believes that cold storage alone is enough. Critics point out that a seed in a freezer is, in effect, frozen in time: unlike a variety still grown in farmers’ fields, it does not continue to evolve as pests and climates change around it. For this reason, many specialists now argue that gene banks should be combined with support for farmers who continue to grow traditional varieties. As Dr Lena Hartwell of the Ardley centre puts it, ‘A seed bank is an insurance policy, not a substitute for diversity that is still alive in the field.’

questions.text: What is said about regeneration at the Ardley centre?

choices.text: It is carried out on every sample once every ten years.
Its managers regard it as the most expensive stage and the one most likely to go wrong.
It is only necessary for plants that cross-pollinate.
It tends to increase the genetic variety within a sample.

questions.explanation: Paragraph E: the managers call it ‘the most costly and risky part of their work’. The ten-yearly check is a germination test (A), maize is only an example (C), and variation may be lost, not gained (D).

questions.text: Why does the writer mention the research centre that left its headquarters in Syria?

choices.text: to show the benefit of keeping copies of seeds in a separate place
to show how war can lead to the looting of gene banks
to suggest that the Arctic vault is used mainly by institutions affected by war

questions.text: What is the main point of the final paragraph?

choices.text: Gene banks have failed to protect the diversity of crops.
Farmers are no longer willing to grow traditional varieties.
Seed samples should be kept in more than one location.
Stored seeds cannot adapt to changing conditions, so other approaches are also needed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph H: frozen seeds do not ‘continue to evolve as pests and climates change’, so banks should be combined with support for farmers. A seed bank is called ‘an insurance policy’, not a failure (A); duplication (C) is the subject of paragraph F.

sections.title: Riding the Monsoon
sections.intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–27, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

texts.heading: Riding the Monsoon
texts.subheading: How seasonal winds created an ocean-wide trading world

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For at least two thousand years, trade across the Indian Ocean ran to a timetable set by the wind. Each year, merchants in ports from the Red Sea to the Bay of Bengal waited for the wind to change direction before setting out on voyages of thousands of kilometres across open water. The sailors who made these journeys came from many backgrounds — Arab, Persian, Indian, East African, Malay and others — and together they built one of the most extensive commercial systems of the pre-modern world.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The key to this system was the monsoon, a word generally thought to derive from the Arabic mawsim, meaning ‘season’. In winter, as the Asian landmass cools, a steady wind blows from the north-east across the Arabian Sea, carrying ships from India and Arabia towards East Africa. In summer the pattern is reversed: as the land heats up, moist air is drawn in from the south-west, bringing the rains on which South Asian farming depends and pushing vessels back towards Arabia and India. Because these winds returned so regularly, a captain could plan the outward and return voyages with some confidence. The system had its limits, however: at the height of the south-west monsoon, seas were so rough that many harbours on India’s western coast effectively closed, so captains sailed at the start or end of the season.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Who first exploited these winds for long-distance voyages is uncertain. Greek and Roman writers of the first century CE credited one of their own navigators with ‘discovering’ that a ship could sail directly across the open sea between the Red Sea and India instead of following the coast. Many modern historians are sceptical. Arab and Indian seafarers, they point out, had almost certainly been using the monsoon long before, and knowledge of this kind is more likely to have accumulated gradually over many generations than to have been revealed to a single individual. The classical account may say more about what was new to its readers than about what was new to the ocean.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The vessels that made these crossings were built in a distinctive way. Whereas Mediterranean shipbuilders generally relied on wooden joints and metal nails, many builders around the western Indian Ocean sewed their planks together with cord made from coconut fibre, threaded through holes drilled along each plank’s edge and pulled tight. Outsiders often found the technique puzzling, and some repeated a legend that magnetic rocks in the ocean would pull the nails out of any ship that used them. The real reasons were almost certainly practical. Coconut fibre was cheap and plentiful around the ocean’s shores, whereas iron was costly in many places and quickly corroded by salt water. A sewn hull was also somewhat flexible, so it could absorb the shock of striking a coral reef or being hauled onto a beach.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Out of sight of land, navigators relied largely on the stars. Since a star’s height above the horizon changes as an observer moves north or south, measuring it showed roughly how far north a ship was. One simple instrument for this purpose was a small wooden board attached to a knotted string. Holding a knot between his teeth and stretching the string tight, the navigator checked whether the board’s lower edge touched the horizon while its upper edge touched the Pole Star; the knot that produced this alignment indicated his latitude. Directions were described using a ‘star compass’, which divided the horizon according to the points where particular stars rose and set. Much of this knowledge was later recorded in Arabic manuals, and one fifteenth-century pilot composed many of his works in verse so that they could be memorised more easily.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Pilots also learned to read the ocean itself. Changes in the colour of the water, the appearance of particular seabirds or sea snakes, and patches of floating vegetation could all warn that land was near, while a weighted line lowered to the seabed revealed both the depth and, from the sand or mud that stuck to it, the nature of the bottom. Such signs allowed an experienced pilot to judge his position even when clouds hid the stars.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The rhythm of the winds shaped communities as well as voyages. Since a ship arriving on one monsoon usually had to wait months for the wind to reverse, merchants spent long periods in foreign ports. Many rented houses, formed partnerships with local traders and married into local families. Over the centuries such settlements produced distinctive cultures, most famously along the coast of East Africa, where the Swahili language absorbed many Arabic words. Gujarati merchants from western India established communities in Arabia and East Africa, while traders from southern Arabia settled as far away as South-East Asia.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The resulting trade worked less like a single highway than like a series of overlapping circuits. Few ships sailed the whole length of the ocean; instead, goods changed hands at busy ports as they passed between regional networks — East African ivory and gold, Arabian frankincense and horses, Indian cotton cloth and pepper, Chinese silk and porcelain. Much of this commerce rested on trust, since merchants routinely extended credit to partners they might not see for years. The Portuguese, arriving in the late 1490s, tried to control the trade by obliging ships to buy passes, but never fully succeeded; wooden sailing vessels still carried cargo across the western Indian Ocean well into the twentieth century.

sections.title: In Defence of Boredom
sections.intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 28–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

texts.heading: In Defence of Boredom
texts.subheading: Could a state of mind we try so hard to escape be good for us?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few states of mind have a worse reputation than boredom. It is associated with wasted time, restless children and unproductive employees, and a vast industry now exists to ensure that we never have to experience it. Waiting for a bus, standing in a queue or sitting through an advertisement, most of us reach for a phone almost without thinking; it has never been easier to banish tedium the moment it appears. Yet a growing body of research suggests that in eliminating boredom so efficiently we may be discarding something of value. The claim deserves careful scrutiny, because it is as easy to romanticise boredom as it is to demonise it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most frequently cited evidence comes from a series of experiments at Calderbridge University led by the psychologist Ines Faulkner. Volunteers were assigned either to a deliberately monotonous task — tracing the outlines of identical circles for twenty minutes — or to an absorbing puzzle of similar length. Both groups then completed a standard test of creative thinking, suggesting as many ways as they could to improve an ordinary household object such as an umbrella. Those who had endured the tedious task produced more ideas, and independent judges rated their ideas as more original. More revealing, however, was a pattern within the bored group: the participants who reported that their minds had wandered most during the task gave the most inventive answers of all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second line of research has looked beyond the laboratory. Tomas Rehn and his colleagues at the Lindqvist Institute equipped 300 adults with a phone app that contacted them at random moments over a fortnight, asking what they were doing, how they felt and what they were thinking about. When participants described themselves as bored, they were considerably more likely than at other times to be thinking about their own futures: their plans, their relationships and whether their current activities were worthwhile. Rehn argues that boredom should be understood as a signal rather than a malfunction. He likens it to the warning light on a car’s dashboard, which does not explain what is wrong but shows that something needs attention: boredom, in his view, tells us that what we are doing no longer serves our goals, and prompts us to look for something more meaningful.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is a plausible mechanism behind both findings. Neuroscientists have identified a network of brain regions that becomes more active when our attention is not occupied by an external task, and which appears to be involved in recalling the past, imagining the future and reflecting on ourselves. It is tempting to conclude that boredom switches this network on, and that this explains both the creativity of Faulkner’s daydreamers and the self-examination of Rehn’s participants. However, the evidence that boredom reliably activates this network remains thin; for now, the link is an attractive hypothesis rather than an established fact. Indeed, Faulkner’s own data imply that what mattered was not boredom as such but the mind-wandering that it allowed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Critics of this research make several serious points. The first concerns the size of the effect. When Priya Nandakumar’s team at Westmere University repeated the Calderbridge procedure with more than a thousand participants, the creative advantage of the bored group was a fraction of that originally reported. The second concerns the kind of boredom being studied. Twenty minutes of tracing circles, the critics argue, bears little resemblance to the chronic, inescapable boredom that some people live with — and it is chronic boredom that has repeatedly been linked to depression, anxiety and addictive behaviour.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third objection is practical. In occupations that require sustained monitoring, such as watching security screens or supervising automated machinery, boredom is associated with lapses of attention that can have serious consequences. There is a moral objection, too. The sociologist Martin Abernethy has observed that praise for boredom tends to come from people who can end it whenever they wish. For a prisoner, or for someone who has been out of work for years, he argues, boredom is not a doorway to creativity but a form of suffering.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: All of these points seem to me correct, and none should be dismissed. The creative benefits of boredom are probably modest; chronic boredom is undoubtedly harmful; and in some jobs a bored worker is a dangerous one. Yet the critics are largely answering a claim that the more careful defenders of boredom do not make. The argument is not that boredom is good in itself, still less that people should seek it out. It is that brief, ordinary boredom carries information — about our goals and about what we might do next — and that our habit of extinguishing it instantly means the message is never received.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What follows from this is a modest proposal. I do not believe that schools should timetable ‘boredom lessons’, or that employers should make work duller in the hope of stimulating innovation; such schemes misunderstand the evidence. The lesson is rather that we might allow a few minutes of boredom to run their course before reaching for a screen, and ask what, if anything, the feeling is trying to tell us. Boredom is not a virtue. But it may be a messenger, and it seems unwise to silence it before it has had a chance to speak.

questions.text: Why does the writer mention the warning light on a car’s dashboard?

choices.text: to suggest that boredom is usually a sign of a serious problem
to show that boredom is very difficult to ignore
to illustrate Rehn’s view that boredom indicates a need for change
to question how reliable Rehn’s interpretation of his data is

questions.explanation: Paragraph C: like the light, which ‘shows that something needs attention’, boredom tells us our activity ‘no longer serves our goals’. Nothing suggests a serious fault (A) or that boredom is hard to ignore (B), and Rehn is not challenged (D).

questions.text: What do the critics in paragraph E say about the boredom produced in laboratory experiments?

choices.text: It is unlike the long-lasting boredom that some people experience.
It is too unpleasant for volunteers to tolerate for long.
It is more likely to cause anxiety than creativity.
It has a stronger effect on creativity than the original study suggested.

questions.explanation: Paragraph E: tracing circles ‘bears little resemblance to the chronic, inescapable boredom’ some people live with. Anxiety is linked to chronic boredom, not the laboratory task (C), and the repeat study found a smaller effect, not a stronger one (D).

questions.text: What is the writer’s view of the critics’ objections?

choices.text: They exaggerate the harm caused by chronic boredom.
They rely on studies that are too small to be reliable.
They show that the case for boredom should be abandoned.
They are mostly aimed at a position that careful defenders of boredom do not hold.

questions.explanation: Paragraph G: the critics are ‘largely answering a claim’ that careful defenders ‘do not make’. The writer still defends brief boredom (C), calls chronic boredom ‘undoubtedly harmful’ (A), and the critics’ own study was large (B).

questions.text: What is the writer’s main purpose in the passage?

choices.text: to describe the findings of one influential experiment
to argue that we should be slower to escape from ordinary boredom
to warn readers about the psychological dangers of long-term boredom
to explain how neuroscience has changed our understanding of boredom

questions.explanation: After weighing the evidence and conceding the critics’ points, the writer concludes that we should let ‘a few minutes of boredom’ run their course before reaching for a screen. A, C and D describe only parts of the passage.
